passages.title: A New Beginning
passages.text:
Moving to a new city is often described as an exciting adventure, but for me, it felt more like a challenge I wasn't ready for. Last summer, my parents announced that we were moving from our quiet village to the bustling city of Manchester. I had lived in the same house for fourteen years, and the thought of leaving my friends and my favourite local park was devastating.

When we first arrived, the noise was the biggest shock. Unlike the peaceful nights I was used to, the city never seemed to sleep. There were sirens, traffic, and people talking at all hours. For the first two weeks, I barely left my room. I felt like an outsider looking in, convinced that I would never fit into this fast-paced environment. I spent most of my time messaging my old friends, feeling sorry for myself.

However, everything changed when I joined a local photography club. I had always enjoyed taking pictures, and I thought it might be a good way to get out of the house. On my first day, I met a girl named Sarah who was also new to the area. We started exploring the city together, looking for interesting buildings and street art to photograph. Through her eyes, I began to see the city differently. Instead of just seeing traffic and noise, I started to notice the beautiful architecture and the vibrant culture.

It has been six months now, and I can honestly say I don't regret the move. While I still miss my old friends, I have built a new life here. I have learned that moving isn't just about changing your address; it is about changing your perspective. You have to be willing to step outside your comfort zone to find the hidden gems in any new place. If you are facing a big move, my advice is to find a hobby or a group that shares your interests. It makes the world feel a lot smaller and much friendlier.

questions.question: How did the writer feel about moving to Manchester at the beginning?
questions.explanation: The writer mentions that the move felt like a challenge they weren't ready for and that they were devastated to leave their friends.
options: a) Excited about the new opportunities.
b) Nervous but ready for a change.
c) Unhappy about leaving their home.
d) Confused by the parents' decision.

questions.question: What was the writer's main problem during the first two weeks?
questions.explanation: The text states the noise was the biggest shock and they felt like an outsider.
options: a) They couldn't find their way around the city.
b) They found the city environment overwhelming.
c) They were struggling with their schoolwork.
d) They had no way to contact their old friends.

questions.question: What helped the writer change their opinion about the city?
questions.explanation: The writer joined a photography club and met a friend who helped them see the city's beauty.
options: a) Their parents forced them to go out more.
b) They found a new school they really liked.
c) They spent more time in the local park.
d) They started a hobby that connected them with others.

questions.question: How does the writer feel about the city after six months?
questions.explanation: The writer says they don't regret the move and have built a new life.
options: a) They are satisfied with their new life.
b) They still wish they had stayed in the village.
c) They are planning to move again soon.
d) They feel the city is still too noisy.

questions.question: What is the writer's main piece of advice for people moving to a new place?
questions.explanation: The writer suggests finding a hobby or group to make the transition easier.
options: a) Try to stay in touch with your old friends as much as possible.
b) Get involved in activities to meet new people.
c) Focus on your studies until you feel at home.
d) Don't worry about the noise of the city.
